description: Lunar Echoes PK is building an interactive dashboard for “Flame in Freefall,” using AI to summarize and rank NASA’s microgravity combustion experiments for fire safety. We welcome teammates in coding, data analysis, AI, and web development. Join us!
summary: Flame Atlas is a web dashboard that summarizes, ranks and interprets 14 NASA microgravity combustion investigations for crew-habitat fire safety. Users choose a habitat (spacecraft, Moon base, equipment developer or model builder) and adjust four scoring weights, so the ranking is transparent and every score can be explained. Each investigation shows its objective, fuel, hardware, test conditions and a key result, and up to three can be compared side by side. An oxygen scale contrasts Earth air (21%), an expected Moon base (30% or more) and a spacesuit (100%). A research-gap panel shows that no partial-gravity combustion data is in PSI yet, and an Earth-applications panel covers water-mist extinguishers, smoke detectors and firefighter gear. An “Ask the atlas” box lets users question Claude, which answers only from the facts on the page. One measured result from BASS-II: a PMMA rod burned in microgravity at 13.6% oxygen versus a 16% normal-gravity limit, so Earth-based flammability limits may not be conservative. Scores are analyst ratings, not NASA measurements, and unknown values are marked “not stated.
details:
What it does
Flame Atlas ranks 14 NASA microgravity combustion investigations (Saffire, BASS, SoFIE, FLARE, SAME, DAFT, FLEX, CFI and the ACME experiments) by how useful they are for crew-habitat fire safety. The user picks a habitat: spacecraft or station, Moon base or rover, equipment developer, or model builder. Each habitat sets four weights: habitat relevance, atmosphere match, modeling value and equipment impact. The user can change the weights with sliders. Every row opens to show the objective, fuel, hardware, test conditions, a key result and exactly why it scored as it did. Up to three investigations can be compared side by side.

Why it matters
The challenge says the data is hard to find, compare and interpret. Flame Atlas gives a ranked, explained starting point. It also shows the Moon-base problem: air there is expected to be 30% oxygen or more, and NASA says that makes materials much more flammable. A research-gap panel states clearly that no partial-gravity combustion data is in PSI yet, and that FM2 and LUCI are expected to add it. An Earth-applications panel covers water-mist extinguishers, smoke detectors and firefighter gear.

The AI part
An “Ask the atlas” box lets users ask Claude questions. It answers only from the facts on the page and says so when the data does not cover a question. The ranking itself is a transparent weighted score, not a black box.

Measured example
From the NASA BASS-II results poster: a 0.25 in PMMA rod burned steadily in microgravity at 13.6% oxygen, while its normal-gravity blow-off limit is 16%. The authors report a negative oxygen margin of safety of 2.4%.

Tools
HTML, CSS and JavaScript in a single web page, with no backend. Built with the help of Claude (AI assistant). Sources: NASA Combustion Science pages, the challenge brief and the BASS-II poster.

Limits we are open about
Scores are our ratings of NASA’s descriptions, not NASA measurements. Many test conditions are marked “not stated” instead of guessed. We could not read the PSI repository directly, so each investigation’s PSI dataset should be confirmed before modeling.
